articles.title: ‘We’re nowhere near done with Framework Laptop 16’ says Framework CEO
articles.summary: The Framework Laptop 16 got little mention at today’s event, which focused on the new, similarly gamer-oriented Framework Desktop instead.
articles.body: Two years ago, the last time Framework had an event in San Francisco, California, the highlight was the Framework Laptop 16 — a laptop promising the “holy grail” of upgradable graphics cards, and easily one of the most ambitious laptops ever made. But today, the Framework Laptop 16 got little mention at its new event, which focused on the new, similarly gamer-oriented Framework Desktop instead. While the Desktop and Framework’s original 13-inch laptop both got the latest AMD processors today, we don’t yet know if or when the Framework Laptop 16 might leap forward too. The only mention of Framework’s flagship laptop was a new “One Key Module” that will experimentally be available for the Framework community to build their own electromechanical keyboards, should they choose to, that would be thin enough to fit in the Laptop 16’s extremely thin Input Module bay. (You can see how the Input Modules work in my video here.) [Image: Framework’s CEO talks about the One Key Module, of which many are embedded in this prototype all-black board. While Framework did finally ship its promised M.2 adapter bay in December, which will let you stick extra SSDs or other peripherals into a Framework Laptop 16 instead of a discrete graphics card, my big question is: is the promising but somewhat problematic laptop a dead end, or will it get new mainboards and new chips in the future? I tracked down Framework CEO Nirav Patel at the event today, and he wouldn’t say much, but he was clear on one thing: “We’re nowhere near done with Framework Laptop 16.” I pushed my luck, asking: Is today the day he can assure us that the Laptop 16 will eventually see at least one GPU upgrade or snap-on secondary battery? “Today is not that day,” he told me. I want to see Framework succeed, and perhaps it’s too early to begin to wonder otherwise — it was still shipping preordered batches of the Laptop 16 to buyers through the middle of last year. But we’ve pushed the company pretty hard on the GPU in the past specifically because it’s a thing rivals have tried and failed at before — Dell/Alienware even got sued over the failed promise of the Alienware Area-51m, which never bothered to ship a second generation of its supposedly upgradable GPUs. Framework has resisted our pushes so far, stopping short of confirming it in our 2023 story: here’s his exact language at the time. It’d be nice if Framework could assure buyers that the upgrades are absolutely coming. But personally, there’s more than a few things about that laptop I’d like to change, and I wouldn’t be surprised if Framework was doing a bit of a rethink even if it does deliver.

articles.title: Supergirl Borrows From the Best, But Milly Alcock’s Great Take on Kara Zor-El Gets Lost in the Spare Parts of Other Movies Used to Tell Her Story
articles.summary: Supergirl mixes a great performance from Milly Alcock with too many half-hearted influences to fly by itself. While Kara's dynamic with her on-screen cousin Superman paints a bright future for the DCU, her solo outing never finds a super-entertaining rhythm.
articles.body:
Supergirl opened in theaters on June 26. It will be available to stream on HBO Max on September 11 .

Walking into Supergirl, I was excited. I had real expectations. Before you even get to the DCU of it all, I’m officially a fan of Craig Gillespie. He’s a guy who makes movies that are all better than you’d think they’d be – Cruella and I, Tonya and Lars and the Real Girl and even The Finest Hours , that boat-broke-in-half rescue movie was surprisingly really good. These are movies that could've easily become forgettable entries in their particular genres, like just another biopic or live-action remake or movie about a guy who’s in love with a sex doll. So the prospect of tackling a superhero movie with that particular ability to elevate a film in an otherwise tired category was intriguing.

Where the DCU is concerned, I’m here for James Gunn’s universe. I’ve liked what’s gone into it so far and I loved Milly Alcock’s first appearance as Kara in her cameo in Superman . I think this version of Supergirl is a blast and her solo outing didn’t do anything to change my mind on that front. But this is also where Supergirl starts to become a tale of two movies. For everything that the movie does right, that thing’s got an alter ego that’s doing it wrong. As a result, the movie is this shuffling, few-steps-forward, few-steps-back kind of slog that never really finds a rhythm.

For example, the reluctant hero thing is actually very difficult to pull off. It’s hard to play “I don’t care” in an engaging way, because if the character on screen doesn’t care, then I certainly don’t care either. Alcock manages it here about as well as you could hope for. Kara’s a mess and there’s no real concern with her ever not being a mess as part of her journey. It’s very fun. The other side of that coin, however, is that she doesn’t have much of a journey. She’s not a markedly different person at the end of the movie than she is at the beginning. Not because of anything she did or didn’t do as a character or an actor, but because the story she’s been put in doesn’t give her much to do and the result is a movie that sort of flattens out and drags.

When she first meets Eve Ridley’s Ruthye, the young girl out for revenge against the man who murdered her entire family, Kara is protective, sticking her neck out to do the right thing for a kid who’s in over her head. By the end of the film, Kara… does exactly the same thing. Part of the point there is that it highlights the impact she has on Ruthye. (Ridley ultimately gets the lion’s share of the character work in the film, and her character’s journey winds up feeling far more complete than Kara’s.) So while Milly Alcock’s performance is a real strength of the movie, and she does pull off the reluctant hero trope, it is still a very familiar trope and the shorthand that’s used in portraying it is a real weakness.

Familiarity in general is another villainous plot Supergirl tries to thwart. On one hand, the movie wears its influences proudly. The comparisons to James Gunn’s work on Guardians of the Galaxy have been obvious since the trailers first dropped, and we knew the True Grit/archetypal Western structure would be a big part of the film because of the source material, Tom King’s Woman of Tomorrow run. A Mad Max influence is just as obvious in the grimy, lifeless terrains and dying worlds on which most of the movie takes place, planets where people scratch for survival. But the old, reliable Mos Eisley Cantina should get a shout-out as well. The alien design and practical makeup FX and costuming throughout the movie are genuinely top shelf, and clearly the customers in Star Wars ’ most wretched hive were on the filmmakers’ minds.

And yet, while I’ll happily take “True Grit meets Mad Max by way of Guardians and Star Wars,” there's still a dulled edge to the whole movie. Instead of taking the post-apocalyptic vibes of Mad Max, they lift a whole plot point straight from Fury Road and handle it, frankly, a little clumsily. And instead of the emotionally relevant needle drops of Guardians, Kara gets slow-paced montages set to a Jimmy Eat World cover that I found… well, it was baffling.

The film's two other headliners fall into these buckets as well. Matthias Schoenaerts as the film’s villain, Krem of the Yellow Hills, looks incredible. His whole appearance would make the creature design team from A New Hope proud. The beads studded into his face, the machinery grafted into his body, the weird little red button he needs to activate to speak, all of it adds up to a striking and genuinely pretty cool image that would have felt at home in the Thunderdome.

But… they don’t ever do anything with it.

Krem, for all the post-apocalyptic biker gang aura he generates, gets nothing else to go on. He has some affectations that Schoenaerts was clearly having a good time with, like how he’s eating something in almost every scene, but that’s all they really are – affectations. There’s nothing that makes him scary or formidable other than a few throwaway lines about his relative strength and the way other people on screen fear him.

Meanwhile, Jason Momoa's Lobo finds his way into the movie as well, and the mostly-impervious anti-hero bounty hunter is just as much fun as fans have been anticipating. Cigar-chomping gets thrown around a little excessively any time a J. Jonah Jameson or a Hellboy or a Will Smith and Jeff Goldblum from Independence Day show up on screen, but Momoa more than earns the descriptor in all the best possible ways in Supergirl. He looks the part as well, with face paint and prosthetics that cut the kind of imposing figure the fan favorite deserves.

Characters come and go in movies, sometimes with very little fanfare, sometimes playing crucial roles in the story. And they don’t always have to be the latter. The issue with Lobo is that he feels a little extra tacked on. The one scene he has with Kara has real reshoot energy . It’s added on to a scene that didn’t need any extra motivation to get to the next scene, nor is he a particularly unique foil for Kara that propels her character in any meaningful way. He just happens to be looking for the same group of guys that Kara and Ruthye are after. The only real added value he gives the movie is a few (admittedly fun) one-liners. And maybe that’s all Lobo needs to be. Ultimately, he shows up to put his immortal stamp of approval on Kara’s actions, but that feels both unnecessary and more than a little pandering, and it leaves me not entirely sure what to do with him.

So the story of this movie continues to be, “they did it right on one hand, but on the other, not so much,” and as just the second entry into Gunn’s DCU, that issue spills over into all the stuff that comes with being a part of a currently-expanding expanded universe. On one hand, Supergirl needs to continue building outwards to some extent, and this is another of the film’s strengths. Her scenes with David Corenswet’s Superman are wonderful. That’s not to say that Superman saved the day here, or that Supergirl needs Superman to be interesting. It’s that the dynamic between the two of them is great – one positively looking toward the future, while the other still nurses old wounds. I’m definitely looking forward to more of this duo on screen .

But on the other hand, where her solo film is concerned, Supergirl needs to flesh out Kara’s backstory. The structure of how and when flashbacks are deployed in Supergirl aside – because my personal preference would have been a straight chronological telling of the story as opposed to stopping in the middle to tell us her backstory – I did find myself way more interested in her time growing up on a floating, life-boat of a city after the destruction of Krypton. There’s work being done there on both fronts, as the film continues to build on the changes made to Kal-El’s origin story from Superman while introducing another side to that story via Kara. The “present day” of the film, with all the cribbing from True Grit and Mad Max and Guardians, feels far less fresh and interesting than Kara's shielded childhood on Argo, even if both have their entertaining moments.

Again though, this is Supergirl’s biggest challenge. There are a lot of things that work throughout this movie, but there are just as many reasons why they don’t quite add up.

articles.title: Tom Holland's Spider-Man 5 Reportedly Has a Director, and It's No Surprise Who It Is
articles.summary: The inevitable Spider-Man: Brand New Day sequel already has its director, according to a fresh report.
articles.body:
The inevitable Spider-Man: Brand New Day sequel already has its director, according to a fresh report.

Deadline has stated that Destin Daniel Cretton will return for Marvel and Sony's fifth Tom Holland-starring Spider-Man movie, after helming this year's box office-breaking Brand New Day.

It's easy to see why everyone involved might be keen for Cretton to return, as Brand New Day nears $2.5 million in ticket sales and becomes the third highest-grossing film of all time. It's also the best box office for a Spider-Man movie ever, and the biggest film of 2026 — at least until Avengers: Doomsday lands this December.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day - Our Biggest Burning Questions

Having said all of that, Cretton has plenty on his plate right now, meaning that his availability had not been assured. Marvel fans have been begging him to make a Shang-Chi sequel for years, which he previously spoke positively about still wanting to do.

But while Shang-Chi 2 may or may not happen, Spider-Man 5 seems a very safe bet. The only issue for Cretton is his own availability, amid an array of other projects he already has lined up including a Hawaii Five-O movie and a live-action Naruto adaptation. Sadly, though, Cretton will no longer be working on a second season of Wonder Man, after Disney's abrupt cancellation of the series.

When could Spider-Man 5 arrive? The earliest gaps in Marvel's release schedule are now not until 2029, when the studio has three untitled movies lined up to launch. (2027 will only feature Avengers: Secret Wars, while 2028 is already stuffed with X-Men, Ghost Rider, and Black Panther 3.) Still, Spider-Man: Brand New Day was filmed last summer for launch less than 12 months after, so it seems possible that Cretton will be able to tick off his other upcoming projects before returning to Spider-Man once more.

As for the franchise's star, Tom Holland has privately discussed returning for several more appearances , though has also said he was now thinking of how to hand over the role to a new Spider-hero . Perhaps Spider-Man 5 is when we finally see a live-action Miles Morales introduced, with Sony's animated Spider-Verse trilogy that features the same character all wrapped up by the time it arrives. Time will tell, though it seems Cretton will be there when cameras do eventually roll.

articles.title: How Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 3 Will Benefit From Tech Improvements Made for John Carpenter's Toxic Commando
articles.summary: John Carpenter's Toxic Commando’s launch came in below publisher Focus Entertainment’s expectations, but for Saber Interactive it was successful in commercial terms — and according to development chief Tim Willits, the tech work done for it will go on to benefit the upcoming Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 3.
articles.body:
John Carpenter's Toxic Commando’s launch came in below publisher Focus Entertainment’s expectations, but for Saber Interactive it was successful in commercial terms — and according to development chief Tim Willits, the tech work done for it will go on to benefit the upcoming Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 3 .

Toxic Commando builds upon Saber’s proprietary tech to present a zombie swarm for co-op players to gun down. It’s technology used for Saber’s World War Z, for the Tyranids in Space Marine 2, and will once again be utilized for the upcoming Space Marine 3.

In its recent financial report, Focus owner Pullup issued a somewhat downbeat note on Toxic Commander, which came out in March. But in an interview with IGN at gamescom, Saber’s Tim Willits was more positive, confirming it was a profitable project for the company.

“We're really happy with it,” he began. “Focus' opinion, they're a publicly traded company, so they have to say what they have to say. We'll leave that to them. But for us, we're really excited about it. We have some new stuff coming out. We actually have a good playerbase.

“It brought more people into the Saber universe. When I say Saber universe, it's people that fall in love with one game who now start to look at us, like Space Marine 2 with our 14 million players. It's f***ing ridiculous. Just a few! And then World War Z, remember that's 30 million people that played that game. It's nuts. More people played that game than saw the movie or read the book.”

Willits went on to say that the tech improvements made for Toxic Commander will be further improved for Space Marine 3. Indeed, you can trace a line from World War Z through Space Marine 2 and Toxic Commando right to Space Marine 3.

Warhammer 40,000 11th Edition Cinematic Trailer: All Shots of the Emperor

“[Toxic] was a well-made game that was fun to play, and it shows people what we do really well,” Willits said. “It shows people that Saber games are enjoyable to experience with your friends. It's over-the-top. It built on our technology. You'll see more of that in Space Marine 3. You can see the progression with our technology moves. I feel that it was a good brick in that Saber wall.

“We're growing the company, we're growing the project, we're growing the technology. It was profitable for us. We don't lose money. We don't lose money on anything.”

I asked Willits how Toxic Commando’s tech will be improved for Space Marine 3, and while he kept his cards close to his chest on actual game features, he did hint at an expanded scope.

“It's the maturity of the technology,” he said. “You can see the bigger swarms, you can see the bigger areas, you can see the better AI. There's cars — you didn’t have cars in Space Marine 2. I'm not saying we're going to have cars in Space Marine 3. I'm just saying the technology is growing and developing and that's our technology. So we can focus on technology pillars that will support our future games like Space Marine 3 and Jurassic Park — that uses the same technology.”

One of the big questions for Space Marine fans is how Saber will expand upon the gameplay. Space Marine 2 limits squads to three characters (modders increased this), and while some of the play spaces are big, there’s nothing you’d describe as having any sort of open world design. Willits has talked about three being the magic number for Space Marine 2 because of the maximum number of enemies it’s able to throw at squads — having four Space Marines, say, would make the game too easy and “scaling enemy assaults to justify bringing a fourth player was too great of a challenge.”

But could Space Marine 3 up the player count by upping the enemy count and playspace? Could it increase the scope of the battles, which in Space Marine 2 are limited in terms of area and units? Willits says he’s not saying Space Marine 3 will have cars, but it does beg the question: will Space Marine 3 have vehicles? A Land Raider, perhaps? Maybe some flying missions in a Gunship?

As for Saber's swarm tech, I'm not sure repeating the trick with Tyranids will be enough for Space Marine 3 after fans spent so much time with them in Space Marine 2. Most believe Space Marine 3 will feature the Necrons, based on hints sprinkled throughout Space Marine 2. But what other factions would fit the bill? A return to the Orks seen in Space Marine 1? (Orks are the primary antagonist of the 11th edition of the Warhammer 40,000 tabletop game.) How about a focus on the relentless Death Guard and swarms of shuffling Plaguebearers? Saber has form when it comes to zombies after all.

As for how Space Marine 3 development is going, Willits was very enthusiastic, but again didn’t give much away. Speaking of how well Space Marine 2 had gone ( he previously told IGN its success had changed everything for Saber ), Willits said the development team was now working to top it.

“The Emperor loves us. We are The Emperor’s favorite,” Willits joked. “All I can say is 3's going great. 2's been really successful. Our DLC's been super successful. People love the mods. It helps the team with experience, knowing what fans actually want, making sure that we adhere to the true Warhammer 40K universe franchise.

“The success of Space Marine 2 has really made the team passionate about making sure that Space Marine 3 is even better. They feel that there's this confidence and passion and vigor, and you can see it. When you talk to the team, they're just in it. So I'm really excited about that.”

Willits recently told IGN that no generative AI was being used in the development of Space Marine 3 , after a backlash online to its use in Saber’s Rideshare Stimulator. Space Marine 3 currently does not have a release window.

articles.title: Nintendo Secures Legal Victory Against Sale of Switch Game Piracy Devices
articles.summary: Nintendo has won a major legal victory aimed at blocking the sale of devices that enable Switch game piracy.
articles.body:
Nintendo has won a major legal victory aimed at blocking the sale of devices that enable Switch game piracy.

The Mario maker has been waging war on the makers of these devices and those who use them over the past few years, and has now turned its attention to the websites that sell them to European customers. Indeed, Nintendo recently took the matter to The District Court of The Hague (note: this is separate to the Hague's International Criminal Court that deals with war criminals) to get their sale deemed unlawful.

Commonly marketed as the MIG Switch, these devices can circumvent Nintendo's anti-piracy measures and play illegal copies of games downloaded from the internet. Nintendo made headlines last year after it began penalizing players who had used these devices on their consoles , disabling the machines' online functionality.

60 The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Switch 2 Screenshots

This new ruling makes it unlawful to sell the MIG Switch and similar devices in Europe in the first place, and specifically names a set of websites where they could be purchased previously. These sites must now cease offering the devices, the court has ordered.

In a statement to press, Nintendo said it had launched this legal action not just to protect its own intellectual property, but also "on behalf of the many video game developers globally that depend on legitimate sales of Nintendo video games.

"Nintendo promotes and fosters game development and creativity and strongly supports the game developers who legitimately create new and innovative games," the company concluded, before issuing a warning directly to fans who might use them:

"Nintendo's message to players is to avoid purchasing or using circumvention devices, circumvention software or unauthorised copies of video games, as this increases the risk of interfering with the functionality and experience provided by authentic Nintendo game consoles, video games and systems."

This is, of course, far from the first time that Nintendo has initiated legal action to stop the sale of piracy-enabling devices. Last year, a Nintendo console modder who refused to shut down his business — and who then attempted to defend himself without a lawyer — was ordered to pay $2 million by Nintendo . And then there's the infamous case of Gary Bowser, an employee of a company that sold anti-piracy devices, who served time in jail and was ordered to pay $14.5m in damages, a debt he's said he will now repay for the rest of his life .

articles.title: PlayStation Ditched Hideo Kojima’s ‘Physint’ on Budget Concerns, Missed Deadlines
articles.summary: The legendary Japanese creator of ‘Death Stranding’ will take his new game to Xbox
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Sony Group Corp.'s PlayStation pulled out of an upcoming game by the well-known designer Hideo Kojima because of concerns over budget, potential profitability and exclusivity, according to people familiar with the project.

One major factor behind the decision was the commercial performance of Kojima's previous two games, Death Stranding and its sequel, which didn't meet PlayStation's revenue expectations, said the people, who asked not to be identified discussing information that's not public.

But the new project has also missed deadlines and was on track to be well over budget despite being years away from release, the people said. In addition, PlayStation was reluctant to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in another game that wouldn't remain permanently exclusive to the company's own hardware. Both Death Stranding games were "timed" PlayStation exclusives that were later released on other platforms. Kojima's closely held studio, Kojima Productions, retained ownership of the franchises.

The new game, Physint, hasn't yet been shown publicly but excited fans when it was announced two years ago with its promise of returning to the "espionage action" genre Kojima pioneered with Metal Gear Solid, the series that propelled him to industry stardom. Kojima surprised fans this week when he announced he would be publishing Physint with PlayStation's biggest rival, Microsoft Corp.'s Xbox.

On Wednesday night, Kojima wrote on social media that over the summer his company had "unexpectedly received notice" that PlayStation was pulling out of funding the game. "Physint is an important project both to me personally and to Kojima Productions," he wrote. "Determined to keep the project alive, we have spent the last three months searching tirelessly for a new partner."

PlayStation also addressed the split on social media, saying it had made the "difficult decision to step away." A representative for PlayStation declined to comment further. A representative for Kojima Productions did not respond to a request for comment. Microsoft said it was "honored" that Kojima chose Xbox and that the two teams plan to collaborate beyond games on films and television, too.

articles.title: Emberville Is a Charming Blend of Stardew Valley and Diablo | IGN Preview
articles.summary: What is here is already an impressive start. Between the mastery and class skill trees, loot, and stat points to distribute, Emberville already appeals to my love of ARPGs, while its gathering and crafting systems have the potential to appeal to a whole different crowd too, like my wife, who is a fan of cozier games. That could make Emberville one of those rare games that we can both enjoy together when it releases and serve as an introduction to the genres for both sides. It's hard to say just yet whether Emberville will be something that draws and keeps me close, like a moth to a flame, or if it will fizzle out like a birthday candle in the wind, but this early look at least shows that this ember is glowing pretty bright.
articles.body:
My demo focused largely on combat, but it nevertheless impressed me.

Emberville’s pixel-art look quickly won me over.

It remains to be seen if its crafting and city-building systems will integrate nicely into Emberville’s whole package.

Described by many as “Diablo meets Stardew Valley,” Cygnus Cross’ debut title, Emberville, is just a little over a month out from welcoming players to check it out. IGN recently had the chance to get an early look, fighting through some mobs, meeting some of its NPCs, and even testing our mettle against an imposing spider boss. All while getting little teases and tastes of the crafting and character depth that we can look forward to when it enters early access in October.

Most of my time with Emberville consisted of fighting through the first biome of the prologue, ending with my arrival in the titular Emberville. After awakening in a strange room, I found my way outside, where a mysterious hooded figure turned me inside-out, leaving a bloody mess of bone and gore where I once stood. I quickly popped back into existence, and thankfully, this time the murder-hungry figure outside was gone, and I could get to exploring. The dungeon-like area I found myself in, which I’d later learn was known as the Vitromotus, serves as a prison and makes those within essentially immortal as they wait out their sentences. Some of these prisoners have even spent so long inside that they have forgotten how long they have been there or lost their memories, requiring special magical devices to help them reclaim what has escaped them.

The story and lore behind what the Vitromotus is, the mysterious magical energy known as Kymia, and even who or what killed me at the start were explained to me through a mix of both talking to NPCs I came across and various books and other notes scattered around the dungeon. Most of that dialogue was voiced, including Alex Jordan’s performance as the elderly and not quite-all-there Adeos, or Matt Mercer’s gremlin-like shopkeeper, Gumu. One of the big selling points that Emberville is pushing is its incredibly robust and talent-rich voice cast that will help give the people of this world life, and while a vast majority of them were not present in the demo, what was there was really well done. I don’t tend to associate A-tier voice acting with games that look like Emberville, so even though I knew going in that the cast was stacked, it was still a pleasant surprise to hear it.

As someone who believes that good pixel art will always be timeless, Emberville’s early dungeon and denizens are right up my alley. With rich and detailed landscapes of dank spiderweb-covered caves, crumbling stone walls, and rotting wooden buildings to rummage through, I have already become enthralled by its graphics. Enemies like the spiders had ominous spotted mushrooms growing on their backs, and I could see the mystic beads dangling from the staves of the acolytes as they conjured their spells to send at me. My character was perhaps the most simplistic-looking element of Emberville, but considering that the various pieces of armor I would equip actually showed up on them – a feature I tend to associate with 3D games, and even then, it doesn’t happen particularly often – it made sense, and the gear itself was detailed and blended in with the rest. I only hope that in the final release you are able to dye your gear as well, to really help with your “drip,” as the kids say. They do still say that, right?

When it came to my character, being rather hooked on the Dungeon Crawler Carl books lately, I decided early on, even while creating my character (which has some decent options for customization), to make a pants-less dude that likes to punch things and step on things, rather than swing a sword or shoot magic spells. Unlike, say, Diablo, which features a single main attack and is backed up by spells or abilities, Emberville has a sort of combo system, where mixing the main and alternate attack buttons in a specific sequence results in a more powerful final hit. In Carl’s case, punching twice – which is the knuckles main attack – and using his alternate kick attack for the final strike in the string would result in a satisfying roundhouse kick that had a chance of leaving the enemies stunned. Throw in the powerful strike I opted for when picking my Wanderer class perk, and I can frequently pull off a satisfying four-hit flurry. That said, I’m still a bit on the fence about it, finding myself wondering if I like it more in principle than in practice.

For smaller groups, and particularly against the large and imposing Spider Matriarch that awaited me at the tail end of the demo, I think this combo approach was pretty neat. On the other hand, when dealing with large mobs or when under pressure, it all went out the window, and I resorted to my tried-and-true frantic clicking to thin the threats around me. Having played the demo on both my PC and my AYN Thor handheld, hitting combos came more naturally for me, alternating face buttons instead of the left and right mouse, so it may just take some time to get used to until it becomes muscle memory. Regardless, it’s certainly a feature that helps set Emberville apart at the very least, I’ve seen enough to be intrigued.

While most of the time was spent throwing hands, I did still try each of the various weapons. Everything from the sword’s swishes and swooshes to the bow's charged shot had a good impact and feel to them, and I appreciated how I could use the staff to either bludgeon foes across the head or blast them with magic. And each of them comes with their own mastery trees that will unlock even stronger attacks should I fight with them, just like with the knuckles. These mastery trees extend not just to weapons either; with the other masteries you can invest in, such as armor, alchemy, and resource gathering, each offering their own benefits.

The scope of the build I got to check out really was combat- and exploration-focused, showing off the looks, enemies, traps, and even the boss of what will serve as the prologue area, but this is just part of what Emberville looks to offer to prospective acolytes when the game launches proper. Emberville is also positioning itself as a solid crafting and even city-building game too. The city and some of its customization have been shown off in previous trailers, but were completely absent in what I got to play, which is a shame.

I did get a slight tease and peek at how crafting and general collection will work, thankfully. Similar to, say, Stardew Valley, or other cozy gathering sims out there, as I explored the Vitromotus, I came across veins to mine for ore, trees to cut down, plants to pull, and other goodies to fill my bag with. Enemies also would drop various components that will no doubt be of great help in brewing bubbling potions or cooking up delicious meals. I occasionally would stumble on a cook fire while exploring, allowing me to do just that, turning raw meat into cooked meals, granting better healing effects. The masteries for all of this, though, weren’t implemented yet, with a “Coming Soon” notice teasing what’s still to come.

Brief as my time was, Emberville still leaves me eager to explore more of its world. The big question now is whether Cygnus Cross can successfully bring all these various systems together into a cohesive package without it feeling like random things just tacked on. The combat already has the bones of a solid ARPG, but I haven't seen enough of the crafting and village-building systems to know whether Emberville's cozier side complements it or just gives the whole thing a bit of an identity crisis, but I'm just as excited to find out as I am to dive deeper into its classes and RPG mechanics.

What is here is already an impressive start. Between the mastery and class skill trees, loot, and stat points to distribute, Emberville already appeals to my love of ARPGs, while its gathering and crafting systems have the potential to appeal to a whole different crowd too, like my wife, who is a fan of cozier games. That could make Emberville one of those rare games that we can both enjoy together when it releases and serve as an introduction to the genres for both sides. It's hard to say just yet whether Emberville will be something that draws and keeps me close, like a moth to a flame, or if it will fizzle out like a birthday candle in the wind, but this early look at least shows that this ember is glowing pretty bright.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto: Vice City – The Legacy Review
articles.summary: The original, legendary GTA: Vice City remains an irresistible experience in 2026 thanks to its unrivalled personality and style, and its sonically unmistakable soundtrack.
articles.body:
Over the next few months, I’m going to be taking a look back at each of the core Grand Theft Auto games and replaying them in the lead-up to the arrival of Grand Theft Auto 6. What we’ll be putting together won’t be traditional re-reviews, and they won’t come with any new IGN score, but they will re-examine what made each GTA remarkable upon the time of its release. By the end of the project, using GTA’s previously six-star wanted level, you should be able to get an idea of where each of these games roughly rank in my long-term love for this series.

Today it’s time to take these broken wings and learn to fly again in Grand Theft Auto: Vice City.

Grand Theft Auto: Vice City is emblematic of a long-extinct era. I’m not actually talking about its famous 1980s setting, though; I’m talking about the games industry at large. While we’ve had to patiently wait more than 12 years between GTA V and GTA VI, 2002’s Vice City arrived first on PlayStation 2 a mere 12 months after the genre-defining GTA III. Nothing as good as Vice City happens this rapidly anymore. And make no mistake – it is very, very good.

Vice City introduces a pile of new vehicle types and weapons, and its missions are immediately more imaginative and varied than its predecessor. It also embraces a noticeably different approach to its storytelling, benching the mute protagonist concept for a fully voiced lead character, giving him the ability to have far more entertaining interactions with a considerably more memorable supporting cast of allies and antagonists. Above everything, however, it oozes unrivalled personality and style thanks to its ’80s backdrop, and is elevated to untouchable heights by its sonically unmistakable soundtrack. I love this game. It grabs me by the crotch and shakes me around until I am not sure if I am a man or a woman. Then I remember I am Luke Reilly – Mister Luke Reilly – and this is Rockstar North with GTA: Vice City.

Realistically, Vice City could have been little more than another serving of the formula that had just completely revolutionised open-world games and it still would’ve sold truckloads. Indeed, for a brief spell, it began life as exactly that. After finalising GTA III on PC, the first thing the team behind it did was begin thinking about what vehicles, weapons, and missions could potentially go into a mission pack for their blockbuster crime sandbox. However, after realising there was too much content to squeeze into an expansion, the next chapter in the GTA saga became a fully fledged sequel instead.

I guess, strictly speaking, the decision to brush aside the present day and place Vice City’s action in 1986 actually makes it a prequel. Whatever you want to call it, it was astounding – and it remains so today.

While GTA III changed the trajectory of the GTA series forever – and set the stage for an entire ecosystem of open world action games to follow – Vice City is notable as the GTA that properly introduced the broader spectrum of vehicle variety we expect from the series today. Motorcycles made their first reappearance since the top-down era, and we could now effectively pilot aircraft – including choppers, and a seaplane with a complete set of wings. It also brought in outfit changes, property purchases, and even an in-game map (although it still came with a paper one, too).

Importantly, however, Vice City also introduced a protagonist with a voice of his own. In GTA III, dialogue typically consists of one-sided monologues – or characters simply barking a batch of mission instructions at you. Vice City is completely different. Thanks to leading man Tommy Vercetti having a voice of his own – provided by iconic Goodfellas star Ray Liotta himself – Vice City is far closer in tone and spirit to the classic crime movies and TV that inspired it in the first place. It’s funnier, snappier, and packed with so much more personality thanks to Tommy’s ability to bite back, express emotion, and give voice to his ambitions. Tommy’s ambition is actually a really important part of the equation, too, and something that further distinguishes Vice City from GTA III. That is, while GTA III is about survival as a little fish in a big pond, Tommy Vercetti is here to become Vice City’s great white shark. Vice City is not about scraping by; Tommy is here to take over this whole town.

Rockstar has since largely pivoted away from casting GTA characters with high-profile film actors, but during Vice City the practice was just about at its peak. Alongside Ray Liotta, Vice City features Tom Sizemore, Dennis Hopper, Burt Reynolds, William Fichtner, Robert Davi, Luis Guzmán, Gary Busey, Lee Majors, Danny Trejo, Danny Dyer, and even Philip Michael Thomas as Lance Vance. Yes, Miami Vice’s legendary Ricardo Tubbs was tapped for a key role in Vice City. Vice City is nothing if not hilariously unapologetic about its reverence for classic Miami crime dramas like Miami Vice and Scarface. It’s certainly no accident that Diaz’s mansion practically still has Al Pacino’s butt print in the office chair, or – if you get your wanted level up to three stars – you’ll be set upon by plain clothes Vice Squad detectives who show up in Cheetah sports cars.

In 2002, Vice City absorbed me immediately. I was obsessed and could not stop playing it. In 2026, I’m hooked all over again. I’d honestly forgotten how great it was to look at, certainly by PS2 standards. I actually don’t know what looks better: the evenings, or the sunrises. I also love all the little flourishes embedded in it – from the glinting ocean chop to the subtle way Tommy’s clothes flap as he whips through the air on a motorcycle. Bikes are such an excellent addition and feel great to ride, and I really dig the way they’re tuned to let you slide them aggressively into corners without abruptly gripping up and high-siding Tommy over the top of them. Cars handle more sharply than GTA III, too, and have a better sense of weight, which is such a crucial part of open-world action games for me.

The combat? Well, I’m still in a love/hate relationship with the general blasting. Yes, the auto targeting is effective in locking on and cutting down your opposition, but only when it’s locking onto your actual opposition – and not your literal allies who you drove to the shootout personally. I just wish it knew the cops directly in front of me are a bigger threat than the distant motorcyclist trying to flee the scene, and it remains an annoying idiosyncrasy of this era of GTA, particularly when it causes me to fail a mission. There are still no mid-mission checkpoints in Vice City, but it does introduce helpful, automated taxi rides back to the start of missions you were just wasted on. By cutting down on repetitive travel, Vice City is not only more respectful of our time, I also think it reduces the risk of players growing to resent particular stretches of the map they otherwise might’ve been forced to drive to and fro across one too many times.

That said, it’s hard for me to grow tired of being in a vehicle in Vice City thanks to the soundtrack, which weaponised licensed music so successfully it single handedly reinvented the etymology of many of these songs in my brain. Can you hear Mister Mister’s Broken Wings without thinking of Fernando Martinez? I can’t. Perhaps the most impressive side effect of having a soundtrack this vast, memorable, and expertly curated is the way it flavours the missions in different ways for different playthroughs. Almost a quarter of a century after playing it for the first time, I found myself in a dirtbike chase through the back alleys of Washington Beach to the pop strains of 99 Luftballons. Not a song I would’ve considered for a frantic, high-speed chase – and yet the uptempo pop jam worked a treat. The fact that you can Baby Driver yourself to an unexpectedly brilliant bit of backing music is one of the GTA series’ greatest strengths, and Vice City is arguably the absolute acme. As far as I’m concerned, it’s not just the best soundtrack of the GTA series – edging out San Andreas and Vice City Stories – it’s one of the best soundtracks in video games full stop.

Vice City occupies a special spot in the history of the series as the first game out of its then-newly rechristened development team, Rockstar North – although it should be noted the studio did have somewhat of a running start. The operation had initially been established as the Edinburgh arm of original GTA creators DMA Design, but DMA’s original Dundee branch had been shuttered shortly after. In other words, the prehistory of Rockstar North stretches back to the founding of DMA in the ’80s – so it’s coincidentally quite fitting its first official project became gaming's most quintessential tribute to that decade.

To be fair to some of the GTA series’ most memorable genre peers, Vice City wasn’t the first open-world action and driving game to use the past as a backdrop. The funkadelic Driver and Driver 2, set in an undefined moment at some point in the late ’70s or early ’80s, rolled back their own clocks some years before Vice City. On top of that, the original Mafia took us on a journey back to the 1930s, during the closing chapter of the United States’ Prohibition era. However, there’s just something richer and more special about the way Vice City transports you back to the beachside, neon-drenched excess of 1986.

There are a combination of elements all working in concert with each other to crank up the atmosphere to irresistible heights. The large fleet of angular exotic supercars and boxy American land whales on the roads, glinting as the beaming sun catches their windscreens. The pedestrians strutting the sidewalks in leather jumpsuits that look like they’ve been peeled directly off Michael Jackson. A bright, sun-kissed cityscape that’s so different to the dense, grimy greys of Liberty City, and which sits atop a seedy underbelly of chainsaw carnage, cartel chaos, cocaine, and cheap porn. The pastel pants, the palm-lined streets, the pulsating soundtrack – all of this in unison made Vice City a magically immersive time capsule like no other game at the time, and like few others since.

I’ve seen it argued that the incredibly successful Vice City served as the primary catalyst for the tidal wave of ’80s nostalgia that followed – ground zero for an exploding obsession with this pastel-powered decade – but I’m not entirely sold on that theory. Don’t get me wrong, Vice City was a genuine cultural juggernaut – but I think it’s better viewed as one significant part of a much broader picture. After all, the back stretch of 1997’s Boogie Nights leaned heavily into the early ‘80s, and The Wedding Singer very famously and successfully transported us back to 1985 when it was released in 1998. 1999’s 200 Cigarettes, 2000’s American Psycho, and 2001’s Wet Hot American Summer also all wound things back to the ’80s prior to the arrival of Vice City. Nostalgia has been powerful and bankable for a long time. Back in the ’90s and 2000s, if we weren’t being whisked back to the ’80s, it was the ’70s, via The Wonder Years, Dazed and Confused, 54, That ‘70s Show, and Detroit Rock City.

No: Rockstar didn’t discover the retro lens with Vice City, nor did it invent ’80s nostalgia. However, all those examples above are movies or TV shows. Vice City is neither. Vice City is a video game, and I probably don’t need to explain to you why that sets it apart. Vice City wasn’t just a window into the past we were restricted to passively peering through for a predefined running time. Rather, it became a living, breathing portal to the past that let us actually explore, experience, and inhabit a long-ended era.

To this day, the opening moments of GTA: Vice City remain one of my most memorable gaming experiences ever. After getting into your first car, you’ll immediately hear the unmistakable bass line of Michael Jackson’s Billie Jean. It’s a small but meaningful moment that instantly plunges you into the past and feels like a happy accident, but it wasn’t – it was engineered to always be Billie Jean. Everyone heard it. Or, at least, they did until later re-issues and remasters of the game unfortunately trimmed it from the soundtrack. Either way, I was completely enchanted by Vice City from that moment. In 2026? I still can’t get enough of it. With its wide variety of vehicles, weapons, and missions, its stacked cast of recognisable voices, and its unmatched atmosphere, Vice City may have gone backwards in time – but it was a huge stride forward for the series and one of my all-time favourites.

For more reflections on the incredible Grand Theft Auto series, you can read our new Legacy Reviews of Grand Theft Auto , Grand Theft Auto 2 , and Grand Theft Auto III , with more to follow over the coming months.

articles.title: A Whisper of Fall: Jinyiwei Brings Serious Martial-Arts Spectacle to Soulslikes | IGN Preview
articles.summary: A Whisper of Fall: Jinyiwei does an impressive job of drawing players into its world of martial-arts action, and I appreciated that it really leaned into the vertical exploration. I would have liked to see more open exploration of towns and communities to understand what the larger world of Jinyiwei is about, but the demo I played is a promising start. It does well to capture that experience of being an action hero, and with later stages focusing on battles within crumbling battleships during storms and all-out brawls while wall-running above death-pits, A Whisper of Fall: Jinyiwei has the makings of an action-RPG that can make an impact with its martial arts action-adventure.
articles.body:
A dedication to martial arts is a key differentiating factor for this soulslike.

It’s reminiscent of the wuxia action of the classic film Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon.

Boss fights should be fairly memorable based on what I’ve experienced so far.

In the wake of this year’s Gamescom, it's been very clear that a wide assortment of new action titles have been looking to make their mark, especially in the soulslike sub-genre. One game in particular that's aiming high is the upcoming action-RPG A Whisper of Fall: Jinyiwei, which brings fast wuxia-inspired combat and spectacle-driven set-piece encounters to the historical Ming Dynasty setting.

We recently got some hands-on time with an early build of this soulslike action-RPG, which blends tense, martial-arts style action from the school of Black Myth: Wukong to the parkour-style action-platforming from Assassin's Creed. So far, A Whisper of Fall: Jinyiwei has a promising hook and serious style that makes a decent first impression, and hopefully it can build on that excitement from here.

The main story of A Whisper of Fall: Jinyiwei follows a mysterious boatman thrust into the political upheaval of the Ming Dynasty, which is in turmoil from encroaching threats both outside the kingdom's walls and within. Taken on as a new agent of the Ming Dynasty, the protagonist becomes the titular Jinyiwei, an imperial agent tasked with striking down invaders and other threats to the kingdom, while expanding his tools and resources to keep the fight going.

Like recent Chinese-developed games such as Swords of Legends or Phantom Blade Zero, A Whisper of Fall: Jinyiwei is built on Chinese historical settings and mythology, channeled into the framework of an action-RPG soulslike. However, compared to the over-the-top spectacle of the aforementioned PBZ, Jinyiwei takes a less fantastical approach and tilts more toward a blockbuster action-thriller. Yet it still leans into that wuxia-inspired influence, with Jinyiwei using different weapons in martial-arts combat, wall-running, and even fighting while wall-running and streaking through the air. It all makes for a slick, visually exciting approach that feels in step with the 2000 wuxia classic Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon.

As mentioned, the build I played of A Whisper of Fall: Jinyiwei was still very much an early showing, but it laid the groundwork for a fast and captivating action game all about taking out foes with style and grace. It really leans into that martial arts action feel. Still, it goes further by making the engagements you have with enemies more about reading their movements so you can effectively take them out as quickly as you can.

My demo focused on the Jinyiwei's infiltration of a mountainside bandit base. As I was exploring it, using wall-runs to reach higher vantage points and finding upper ledges to get the drop on enemies, it really reminded me of a type of stealth-action game from the Assassin's Creed series, and even with the fairly modest level design, I did appreciate that A Whisper of Fall still presented different ways to go about engaging in battles. In one instance, I encountered a group of three foes on patrol. While the direct approach was doable, I found it better to pick off two enemies from above with a leap-down attack, letting me mop up the last enemy quickly.

The flow of these battles matches the pacing of other, more grounded soulslikes. Still, in keeping with the martial-arts action influence, the protagonist can use his intuition to land critical strikes after evading and whittling down defenses. It captures that feeling of being a badass martial artist, using quick reflexes and your ability to read an opponent to effortlessly take down enemies. During battle, the Jinyiwei can also charge up internal energy based on his performance. Along with using that energy to restore health when you are in a pinch, you can use a fully charged meter for a special attack to tear into enemy and boss defenses, which is super satisfying to nail.

Along with getting new armor to deck out his appearance and defenses, the Jinyiwei can acquire new weapons and can carry two in battle, which can be switched off from each other in mid-combo. I used the traditional Chinese straight sword and a curved bandit sword, swapping between them with special weapon attacks that lead into a new combo. In my experience so far, the combat has a satisfying flow. However, I hope the developers can keep refining and polishing the experience, as one recurring issue was disruptive camera angles that reared their ugly heads during some of the tougher battles.

Where A Whisper of Fall: Jinyiwei really goes all in for its spectacle fights is with the boss encounters. Instead of large monsters and other oversized enemies, the boss gauntlet I got to experience was against other equally matched martial artists who had unique fighting styles, such as a rival mercenary who uses his long sword to create razor-sharp gusts of wind and tosses homing darts to pick me off from a distance. The final boss of the demo was the bandit leader, who then revealed his true form as a fiery, flamesword-wielding warlord. It was a tough fight to get through, but it was all about patience and not getting overwhelmed.

As challenging as these bosses were, what really stood out for me was how evenly matched most of these fights were. There was never that awkward dance of having to figure out the big puzzle of the fight to survive – such as which targets to strike first to open their defenses up. It was really about keeping your composure and reading their movement style to stay ahead of them and steadily cut them down to size with carefully laid-out counterstrikes and parries. It has the fundamentals of satisfying boss encounters, and I hope the larger game will keep building that pacing further.

A Whisper of Fall: Jinyiwei does an impressive job of drawing players into its world of martial-arts action, and I appreciated that it really leaned into the vertical exploration. I would have liked to see more open exploration of towns and communities to understand what the larger world of Jinyiwei is about, but the demo I played is a promising start. It does well to capture that experience of being an action hero, and with later stages focusing on battles within crumbling battleships during storms and all-out brawls while wall-running above death-pits, A Whisper of Fall: Jinyiwei has the makings of an action-RPG that can make an impact with its martial arts action-adventure.

articles.title: PlayStation Ditched Kojima's Physint Due to Missed Deadlines and Budget Concerns, Report Claims
articles.summary: Sony's decision to walk away from its deal with the legendary Metal Gear Solid creator Hideo Kojima for upcoming PlayStation game Physint was reportedly the result of budget concerns and missed deadlines.
articles.body:
Sony's decision to walk away from its deal with the legendary Metal Gear Solid creator Hideo Kojima for upcoming PlayStation game Physint was reportedly the result of budget concerns and missed deadlines.

That's according to a fresh Bloomberg report that details some of Sony's thinking behind the decision to walk away from Physint , which Microsoft subsequently snapped up for Xbox.

As suggested yesterday by analysts speaking to IGN in the aftermath of the news breaking , Sony appears to be reigning in its spending after a woeful run of first-party game flops and cancellations. After wasting hundreds of millions of dollars developing the short-lived Concord, Naughty Dog's now-canned The Last of Us Online, and the still-limping Marathon, Sony is apparently enforcing stricter production milestones.

Bloomberg's report includes the direct assertion that Physint "missed deadlines and was on track to be well over budget despite being years away from release," according to the publication's sources.

The revenue performance of Death Stranding and its sequel, another factor previously mentioned by analysts, also played a part in Sony's decision, it's claimed. While the first title turned a profit for Kojima Productions, Death Stranding 2 failed to build on this success.

Analysis from Alinea Analytics previously suggested that Death Stranding 2 sales have now slowed to a trickle, that several notable discounts on the game have failed to move the needle, and that revenue for the game remains far lower than that of its predecessor.

Several other factors also came into play for Sony, Bloomberg's report continues. One is Sony's previously-reported decision to stop releasing many of its single-player games on PC — something that would have cut into Physint's potential audience further. And another reason is apparently that, while Kojima and PlayStation have enjoyed a long partnership together since the days of PS1, many of the Sony chiefs who previously worked with the Metal Gear creator have since moved on.

With Kojima cut adrift, the report closes with details on why Xbox immediately swooped in, other than to secure the obvious PR win of nabbing Kojima from PlayStation. It's claimed that Xbox's new leaders under boss Asha Sharma saw Physint as a strong investment, with plans to launch the game on PC (no surprise there) and as an alignment with Sharma's stated goal of expanding Xbox's reach beyond games to film and TV. As part of Sony and Kojima's original announcement, some form of movie studio involvement was teased — though exactly what's being planned, we're still waiting to hear.

"This doesn't look great for PlayStation among core gamers," Alinea Analytics analyst Rhys Elliot said yesterday. "Especially right now. From a strictly financial perspective, though, I can understand Sony’s position. In a vacuum, anyway.

Next up from Kojima will be OD, the PT-like project already confirmed as coming to Xbox. As of yet, there's no word on when that will arrive, let alone Physint — though the latter has been described as a next-gen game.
